{{Short description|Generalization of a polytope in real space}}
{{Dark mode problems}}
In [[geometry]], a '''complex polytope''' is a generalization of a [[polytope]] in [[real coordinate space|real space]] to an analogous structure in a [[Complex number|complex]] [[Hilbert space]], where each real dimension is accompanied by an [[imaginary number|imaginary]] one.

A complex polytope may be understood as a collection of complex points, lines, planes, and so on, where every point is the junction of multiple lines, every line of multiple planes, and so on.

Precise definitions exist only for the [[#Regular complex polytopes|regular complex polytopes]], which are [[Configuration (polytope)|configurations]]. The regular complex polytopes have been completely characterized, and can be described using a symbolic notation developed by [[Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter|Coxeter]].

Some complex polytopes which are not fully regular have also been described.

== Definitions and introduction ==
The '''complex line''' <math>\mathbb{C}^1</math> has one dimension with [[real number|real]] coordinates and another with [[imaginary number|imaginary]] coordinates. Applying real coordinates to both dimensions is said to give it two dimensions over the real numbers. A real plane, with the imaginary axis labelled as such, is called an [[Argand diagram]]. Because of this it is sometimes called the complex plane. Complex 2-space (also sometimes called the complex plane) may be considered as a [[four-dimensional space]] over the reals. Likewise, complex n-space may be viewed as a real 2n-dimensional vector space.

A complex ''n''-polytope in complex ''n''-space is the analogue of a real ''n''-[[polytope]] in real ''n''-space. However, there is no natural complex analogue of the ordering of points on a real line (or of the associated combinatorial properties). Because of this a complex polytope cannot be seen as a contiguous surface and it does not bound an interior in the way that a real polytope does.

In the case of ''regular'' polytopes, a precise definition can be made by using the notion of symmetry. For any [[regular polytope]] the symmetry group (here a [[complex reflection group]], called a [[Shephard group]]) acts transitively on the [[flag (geometry)|flags]], that is, on the nested sequences of a point contained in a line contained in a plane and so on.

More fully, say that a collection ''P'' of affine subspaces (or ''flats'') of a complex [[unitary space]] ''V'' of dimension ''n'' is a regular complex polytope if it meets the following conditions:<ref>[[Peter Orlik]], Victor Reiner, Anne V. Shepler. [http://www.math.unt.edu/~ashepler/papers/ORS.pdf ''The sign representation for Shephard groups'']. ''Mathematische Annalen''. March 2002, Volume 322, Issue 3, pp. 477–492. DOI:10.1007/s002080200001</ref>{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=115}}
* for every {{math| −1 ≤ ''i'' < ''j'' < ''k'' ≤ ''n''}}, if {{math|''F''}} is a flat in ''P'' of dimension ''i'' and {{math|''H''}} is a flat in ''P'' of dimension ''k'' such that {{math|''F'' ⊂ ''H''}} then there are at least two flats ''G'' in ''P'' of dimension ''j'' such that {{math|''F'' ⊂ ''G'' ⊂ ''H''}};
* for every {{math| ''i'', ''j''}} such that {{math| −1 ≤ ''i'' < ''j'' − 2, ''j'' ≤ ''n''}}, if {{math|''F'' ⊂ ''G''}} are flats of ''P'' of dimensions ''i'', ''j'', then the set of flats between ''F'' and ''G'' is connected, in the sense that one can get from any member of this set to any other by a sequence of containments; and
* the subset of unitary transformations of ''V'' that fix ''P'' are transitive on the ''flags'' {{math| ''F''<sub>0</sub> ⊂ ''F''<sub>1</sub> ⊂ … ⊂''F''<sub>''n''</sub>}} of flats of ''P'' (with {{math| ''F''<sub>''i''</sub>}} of dimension ''i'' for all ''i'').

(Here, a flat of dimension −1 is taken to mean the [[empty set]].)  Thus, by definition, regular complex polytopes are [[configuration (polytope)|configurations]] in complex unitary space.<ref>Shephard (1952), p. 83</ref>

The '''regular complex polytopes''' were discovered by [[Geoffrey Colin Shephard|Shephard]] (1952), and the theory was further developed by Coxeter (1974).

In the left image, the outlined squares are not elements of the polytope but are included merely to help identify vertices lying in the same complex line. The octagonal perimeter of the left image is not an element of the polytope, but it is a [[Petrie polygon]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|at=11.3 ''Petrie Polygon'', a simple ''h''-gon formed by the orbit of the flag (O<sub>0</sub>,O<sub>0</sub>O<sub>1</sub>) for the product of the two generating reflections of any nonstarry regular complex polygon, ''p''<sub>1</sub>{''q''}''p''<sub>2</sub>}} In the middle image, each edge is represented as a real line and the four vertices in each line can be more clearly seen. 
|[[File:Complex polygon 4-4-2-perspective-labeled.svg|160px]]<BR>A perspective sketch representing the 16 vertex points as large black dots and the 8 4-edges as bounded squares within each edge. The green path represents the octagonal perimeter of the left hand image.
|}

A complex polytope exists in the complex space of equivalent dimension. For example, the vertices of a '''complex polygon''' are points in the complex plane <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math> (a plane in which each point has two complex numbers as its coordinates, not to be confused with the [[Argand plane]] of complex numbers), and the edges are complex lines <math>\mathbb{C}^1</math> existing as (affine) subspaces of the plane and intersecting at the vertices. Thus, as a one-dimensional complex space, an edge can be given its own [[coordinate system]], within which the points of the edge are each represented by a single complex number. 

In a regular complex polytope the vertices incident on the edge are arranged symmetrically about their [[centroid]], which is often used as the origin of the edge's coordinate system (in the real case the centroid is just the midpoint of the edge). The symmetry arises from a [[complex reflection]] about the centroid; this reflection will leave the [[Complex number#Absolute value and argument|magnitude]] of any vertex unchanged, but change its [[Complex number#Absolute value and argument|argument]] by a fixed amount, moving it to the coordinates of the next vertex in order. So we may assume (after a suitable choice of scale) that the vertices on the edge satisfy the equation <math>x^p - 1 = 0</math> where ''p'' is the number of incident vertices. Thus, in the Argand diagram of the edge, the vertex points lie at the vertices of a [[regular polygon]] centered on the origin.

Three real projections of regular complex polygon 4{4}2 are illustrated above, with edges ''a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h''. It has 16 vertices, which for clarity have not been individually marked. Each edge has four vertices and each vertex lies on two edges, hence each edge meets four other edges. In the first diagram, each edge is represented by a square. The sides of the square are ''not'' parts of the polygon but are drawn purely to help visually relate the four vertices. The edges are laid out symmetrically. (Note that the diagram looks similar to the [[Tesseract#2D orthographic projections|B<sub>4</sub> Coxeter plane projection]] of the [[tesseract]], but it is structurally different).

The middle diagram abandons octagonal symmetry in favour of clarity. Each edge is shown as a real line, and each meeting point of two lines is a vertex. The connectivity between the various edges is clear to see.

The last diagram gives a flavour of the structure projected into three dimensions: the two cubes of vertices are in fact the same size but are seen in perspective at different distances away in the fourth dimension.

== Regular complex one-dimensional polytopes ==
[[File:Complex 1-topes as k-edges.svg|thumb|640px|Complex 1-polytopes represented in the [[Argand plane]] as regular polygons for ''p'' = 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, with black vertices. The centroid of the ''p'' vertices is shown seen in red. The sides of the polygons represent one application of the symmetry generator, mapping each vertex to the next counterclockwise copy. These polygonal sides are not edge elements of the polytope, as a complex 1-polytope can have no edges (it often ''is'' a complex edge) and only contains vertex elements.]]
A real 1-dimensional polytope exists as a closed segment in the real line <math>\mathbb{R}^1</math>, defined by its two end points or vertices in the line. Its [[Schläfli symbol]] is {} .

Analogously, a complex 1-polytope exists as a set of ''p'' vertex points in the complex line <math>\mathbb{C}^1</math>. These may be represented as a set of points in an [[Argand diagram]] (''x'',''y'')=''x''+''iy''. A [[regular polygon|regular]] complex 1-dimensional polytope <sub>''p''</sub>{} has ''p'' (''p'' ≥ 2) vertex points arranged to form a convex [[regular polygon]] {''p''} in the Argand plane.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=103|at=11.1 ''Regular complex polygons''}}

Unlike points on the real line, points on the complex line have no natural ordering. Thus, unlike real polytopes, no interior can be defined.<ref>Shephard, 1952; ''"It is from considerations such as these that we derive the notion of the interior of a polytope, and it will be seen that in unitary space where the numbers cannot be so ordered such a concept of interior is impossible. [Para break] Hence ... we have to consider unitary polytopes as configurations."''</ref> Despite this, complex 1-polytopes are often drawn, as here, as a bounded regular polygon in the Argand plane.

[[File:Coxeter_node_markup_real_unitary.png|thumb|A real edge is generated as the line between a point and its reflective image across a mirror. A unitary reflection order 2 can be seen as a 180 degree rotation around a center. An edge is ''inactive'' if the generator point is on the reflective line or at the center.]]
A [[regular polygon|regular]] real 1-dimensional polytope is represented by an empty [[Schläfli symbol]] {}, or [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]] {{CDD|node_1}}. The dot or node of the Coxeter-Dynkin diagram itself represents a reflection generator while the circle around the node means the generator point is not on the reflection, so its reflective image is a distinct point from itself. By extension, a regular complex 1-dimensional polytope in <math>\mathbb{C}^1</math> has [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]] {{CDD|pnode_1}}, for any [[Natural number|positive integer]] ''p'', 2 or greater, containing ''p'' vertices. ''p'' can be suppressed if it is 2. It can also be represented by an empty [[Schläfli symbol]] <sub>''p''</sub>{}, }<sub>''p''</sub>{, {}<sub>''p''</sub>, or <sub>''p''</sub>{2}<sub>1</sub>. The 1 is a notational placeholder, representing a nonexistent reflection, or a period 1 identity generator. (A 0-polytope, real or complex is a point, and is represented as } {, or <sub>1</sub>{2}<sub>1</sub>.)

The symmetry is denoted by the [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|pnode}}, and can alternatively be described in [[Coxeter notation]] as <sub>''p''</sub>[], []<sub>''p''</sub> or ]<sub>''p''</sub>[, <sub>''p''</sub>[2]<sub>1</sub> or <sub>''p''</sub>[1]<sub>''p''</sub>. The symmetry is isomorphic to the [[cyclic group]], order ''p''.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=96}} The subgroups of <sub>''p''</sub>[] are any whole divisor ''d'', <sub>''d''</sub>[], where ''d''≥2.

A [[unitary operator]] generator for {{CDD|pnode}} is seen as a rotation by 2&pi;/''p'' radians [[counter clockwise]], and a {{CDD|pnode_1}} edge is created by sequential applications of a single unitary reflection. A unitary reflection generator for a 1-polytope with ''p'' vertices is {{math| ''e''<sup>2&pi;''i''/''p''</sup> {{=}} cos(2&pi;/''p'') + ''i'' sin(2&pi;/''p'')}}. When ''p'' = 2, the generator is ''e''<sup>&pi;''i''</sup> = –1, the same as a [[point reflection]] in the real plane.

In higher complex polytopes, 1-polytopes form ''p''-edges. A 2-edge is similar to an ordinary real edge, in that it contains two vertices, but need not exist on a real line.

== Regular complex polygons ==
{{main|Regular complex polygon}}
While 1-polytopes can have unlimited ''p'', finite regular complex polygons, excluding the double prism polygons <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub>, are limited to 5-edge (pentagonal edges) elements, and infinite regular apeirogons also include 6-edge (hexagonal edges) elements.

=== Notations ===

==== Shephard's modified Schläfli notation ====
[[Geoffrey Colin Shephard|Shephard]] originally devised a modified form of [[Schläfli symbol|Schläfli's notation]] for regular polytopes. For a polygon bounded by ''p''<sub>1</sub>-edges, with a ''p''<sub>2</sub>-set as vertex figure and overall symmetry group of order ''g'', we denote the polygon as ''p''<sub>1</sub>(''g'')''p''<sub>2</sub>.

The number of vertices ''V'' is then ''g''/''p''<sub>2</sub> and the number of edges ''E'' is ''g''/''p''<sub>1</sub>.

The complex polygon illustrated above has eight square edges (''p''<sub>1</sub>=4) and sixteen vertices (''p''<sub>2</sub>=2). From this we can work out that ''g'' = 32, giving the modified Schläfli symbol 4(32)2.

==== Coxeter's revised modified Schläfli notation ====
A more modern notation <sub>''p''<sub>1</sub></sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub> is due to [[Coxeter]],{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=xiv}} and is based on [[group theory]]. As a symmetry group, its symbol is <sub>''p''<sub>1</sub></sub>[''q'']<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub>.

The symmetry group <sub>''p''<sub>1</sub></sub>[''q'']<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub> is represented by 2 generators R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, where: R<sub>1</sub><sup>''p''<sub>1</sub></sup> = R<sub>2</sub><sup>''p''<sub>2</sub></sup> = I. If ''q'' is even, (R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>''q''/2</sup> = (R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>''q''/2</sup>. If ''q'' is odd, (R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>(q−1)/2</sup>R<sub>2</sub> = (R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>(''q''−1)/2</sup>R<sub>1</sub>. When ''q'' is odd, ''p''<sub>1</sub>=''p''<sub>2</sub>.

For <sub>4</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub> has R<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup> = R<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> = I, (R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup> = (R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>.

For <sub>3</sub>[5]<sub>3</sub> has R<sub>1</sub><sup>3</sup> = R<sub>2</sub><sup>3</sup> = I, (R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup>R<sub>2</sub> = (R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>R<sub>1</sub>.

==== Coxeter-Dynkin diagrams ====
Coxeter also generalised the use of [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]]s to complex polytopes, for example the complex polygon <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> is represented by {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode}} and the equivalent symmetry group, <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''r''</sub>, is a ringless diagram {{CDD|pnode|q|rnode}}. The nodes ''p'' and ''r'' represent mirrors producing ''p'' and ''r'' images in the plane. Unlabeled nodes in a diagram have implicit 2 labels. For example, a real [[regular polygon]] is <sub>2</sub>{''q''}<sub>2</sub> or {''q''} or {{CDD|node_1|q|node}}.

One limitation, nodes connected by odd branch orders must have identical node orders. If they do not, the group will create "starry" polygons, with overlapping element. So {{CDD|3node_1|4|node}} and {{CDD|3node_1|3|3node}} are ordinary, while {{CDD|4node_1|3|node}} is starry.

==== 12 Irreducible Shephard groups ====
[[File:Rank2_shephard_subgroups.png|thumb|12 irreducible Shephard groups with their subgroup index relations.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=177|at=Table III}} Subgroups index 2 relate by removing a real reflection:<BR><sub>''p''</sub>[2''q'']<sub>2</sub> → <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''p''</sub>, index 2.<BR><sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>''q''</sub> → <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''p''</sub>, index ''q''.]]
[[File:Rank2_shephard_subgroups2_series.png|thumb|<sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub> subgroups: p=2,3,4...<BR><sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub> → [''p''], index ''p''<BR><sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub> → <sub>''p''</sub>[]×<sub>''p''</sub>[], index 2]]
Coxeter enumerated this list of regular complex polygons in <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math>. A regular complex polygon, <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> or {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode}}, has ''p''-edges, and ''r''-gonal [[vertex figure]]s. <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> is a finite polytope if (''p''+''r'')''q''>''pr''(''q''-2).

Its symmetry is written as <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''r''</sub>, called a ''[[Shephard group]]'', analogous to a [[Coxeter group]], while also allowing [[unitary reflection]]s.

For nonstarry groups, the order of the group <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''r''</sub> can be computed as <math>g = 8/q \cdot (1/p+2/q+1/r-1)^{-2}</math>.<ref>Lehrer & Taylor 2009, p. 87</ref>

The [[Coxeter number]] for <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''r''</sub> is  <math>h = 2/(1/p+2/q+1/r-1)</math>, so the group order can also be computed as <math>g = 2h^2/q</math>. A regular complex polygon can be drawn in orthogonal projection with ''h''-gonal symmetry.

The rank 2 solutions that generate complex polygons are:

Excluded solutions with odd ''q'' and unequal ''p'' and ''r'' are: <sub>6</sub>[3]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>6</sub>[3]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>9</sub>[3]<sub>3</sub>, <sub>12</sub>[3]<sub>3</sub>, ..., <sub>5</sub>[5]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>6</sub>[5]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>8</sub>[5]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>9</sub>[5]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>4</sub>[7]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>9</sub>[5]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>3</sub>[9]<sub>2</sub>, and <sub>3</sub>[11]<sub>2</sub>.

Other whole ''q'' with unequal ''p'' and ''r'', create starry groups with overlapping fundamental domains: {{CDD|3node|3|node}}, {{CDD|4node|3|node}}, {{CDD|5node|3|node}}, {{CDD|5node|3|3node}}, {{CDD|3node|5|node}}, and {{CDD|5node|5|node}}.

The [[dual polygon]] of <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> is <sub>''r''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''</sub>. A polygon of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''</sub> is self-dual. Groups of the form <sub>''p''</sub>[2''q'']<sub>2</sub> have a half symmetry <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''p''</sub>, so a regular polygon {{CDD|pnode_1|3|2x|q|3|node}} is the same as quasiregular {{CDD|pnode_1|3|q|3|pnode_1}}. As well, regular polygon with the same node orders, {{CDD|pnode_1|3|q|3|pnode}}, have an [[Alternation (geometry)|alternated]] construction {{CDD|node_h|3|2x|q|3|pnode}}, allowing adjacent edges to be two different colors.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=178–179|at=Table IV. The regular polygons}}

The group order, ''g'', is used to compute the total number of vertices and edges. It will have ''g''/''r'' vertices, and ''g''/''p'' edges. When ''p''=''r'', the number of vertices and edges are equal. This condition is required when ''q'' is odd.

==== Matrix generators ====
The group ''p''[''q'']''r'', {{CDD|pnode|q|rnode}}, can be represented by two matrices:{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=88|at=Sec. 8.9 ''The Two-Dimensional Case''}}

|''r''

<math>\left [\begin{smallmatrix}
e^{2\pi i/p} & 0 \\
(e^{2\pi i/p}-1)k & 1 \\
\end{smallmatrix}\right ]

<math>\left [\begin{smallmatrix}
1 & (e^{2\pi i/r}-1)k \\
0 & e^{2\pi i/r} \\
\end{smallmatrix}\right ]
</math>
|}
With
: <math> k = \sqrt \frac{ \cos(\frac{\pi}{p}-\frac{\pi}{r})+\cos(\frac{2\pi}{q}) }{2\sin\frac{\pi}{p}\sin\frac{\pi}{r} } </math>

=== Visualizations of regular complex polygons ===
Polygons of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{2''r''}<sub>''q''</sub> can be visualized by ''q'' color sets of ''p''-edge. Each ''p''-edge is seen as a regular polygon, while there are no faces.

;2D orthogonal projections of complex polygons <sub>2</sub>{''r''}<sub>''q''</sub>:

Polygons of the form <sub>2</sub>{4}<sub>''q''</sub> are called generalized [[orthoplex]]es. They share vertices with the 4D ''q''-''q'' [[duopyramid]]s, vertices connected by 2-edges.

;Complex polygons <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub>:

Polygons of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub> are called generalized [[hypercube]]s (squares for polygons). They share vertices with the 4D ''p''-''p'' [[duoprism]]s, vertices connected by p-edges. Vertices are drawn in green, and ''p''-edges are drawn in alternate colors, red and blue. The perspective is distorted slightly for odd dimensions to move overlapping vertices from the center.

;2D orthogonal projections of complex polygons, <sub>''p''</sub>{''r''}<sub>''p''</sub>:

Polygons of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{''r''}<sub>''p''</sub> have equal number of vertices and edges. They are also self-dual.

== Regular complex polytopes ==
In general, a '''regular complex polytope''' is represented by Coxeter as <sub>''p''</sub>{''z''<sub>1</sub>}<sub>''q''</sub>{z<sub>2</sub>}<sub>''r''</sub>{z<sub>3</sub>}<sub>''s''</sub>... or Coxeter diagram {{CDD|pnode_1|3|z|1x|3|qnode|3|z|2x|3|rnode|3|z|3x|3|snode}}..., having symmetry <sub>''p''</sub>[''z''<sub>1</sub>]<sub>''q''</sub>[''z''<sub>2</sub>]<sub>''r''</sub>[''z''<sub>3</sub>]<sub>''s''</sub>... or {{CDD|pnode|3|z|1x|3|qnode|3|z|2x|3|rnode|3|z|3x|3|snode}}....{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp= 116–140}}

There are infinite families of regular complex polytopes that occur in all dimensions, generalizing the [[hypercube]]s and [[cross polytope]]s in real space.  Shephard's "generalized orthotope" generalizes the hypercube; it has symbol given by &gamma;{{supsub|''p''|''n''}} = <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub>{3}<sub>2</sub>...<sub>2</sub>{3}<sub>2</sub> and diagram {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|3|node|3|node|3}}...{{CDD|node|3|node|3|node}}.  Its symmetry group has diagram <sub>''p''</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub>[3]<sub>2</sub>...<sub>2</sub>[3]<sub>2</sub>; in the Shephard–Todd classification, this is the group G(''p'', 1, ''n'') generalizing the signed permutation matrices. Its dual regular polytope, the "generalized cross polytope", is represented by the symbol &beta;{{supsub|''p''|''n''}} = <sub>2</sub>{3}<sub>2</sub>{3}<sub>2</sub>...<sub>2</sub>{4}<sub>''p''</sub> and diagram {{CDD|node_1|3|node|3|node|3|node|3}}...{{CDD|3|node|4|pnode}}.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=118–119}}

A 1-dimensional ''regular complex polytope'' in <math>\mathbb{C}^1</math> is represented as {{CDD|pnode_1}}, having ''p'' vertices, with its [[real representation]] a [[regular polygon]], {''p''}. Coxeter also gives it symbol &gamma;{{supsub|p|1}} or &beta;{{supsub|p|1}} as 1-dimensional generalized hypercube or cross polytope. Its symmetry is <sub>''p''</sub>[] or {{CDD|pnode}}, a cyclic group of order ''p''.  In a higher polytope, <sub>''p''</sub>{} or {{CDD|pnode_1}} represents a ''p''-edge element, with a 2-edge, {} or {{CDD|node_1}}, representing an ordinary real edge between two vertices.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=118–119}}

A '''dual complex polytope''' is constructed by exchanging ''k'' and (''n''-1-''k'')-elements of an ''n''-polytope. For example, a dual complex polygon has vertices centered on each edge, and new edges are centered at the old vertices. A ''v''-valence vertex creates a new ''v''-edge, and ''e''-edges become ''e''-valence vertices.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=29}} The dual of a regular complex polytope has a reversed symbol. Regular complex polytopes with symmetric symbols, i.e. <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''</sub>, <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''</sub>, <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub>{''s''}<sub>''r''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''</sub>, etc. are '''self dual'''.

=== Enumeration of regular complex polyhedra ===
[[File:Rank3_shephard_subgroups.png|thumb|Some rank 3 Shephard groups with their group orders, and the reflective subgroup relations]]
Coxeter enumerated this list of nonstarry regular complex polyhedra in <math>\mathbb{C}^3</math>, including the 5 [[platonic solid]]s in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=180|at=Table V. The nonstarry regular polyhedra and 4-polytopes}}

A regular complex polyhedron, <sub>''p''</sub>{''n''<sub>1</sub>}<sub>''q''</sub>{''n''<sub>2</sub>}<sub>''r''</sub> or {{CDD|pnode_1|3|n|1x|3|qnode|3|n|2x|3|rnode}}, has {{CDD|pnode_1|3|n|1x|3|qnode}} faces, {{CDD|pnode_1}} edges, and {{CDD|qnode_1|3|n|2x|3|rnode}} [[vertex figure]]s.

A complex regular polyhedron <sub>''p''</sub>{''n''<sub>1</sub>}<sub>''q''</sub>{''n''<sub>2</sub>}<sub>''r''</sub> requires both ''g''<sub>1</sub> = order(<sub>''p''</sub>[''n''<sub>1</sub>]<sub>''q''</sub>) and ''g''<sub>2</sub> = order(<sub>''q''</sub>[''n''<sub>2</sub>]<sub>''r''</sub>) be finite.

Given ''g'' = order(<sub>''p''</sub>[''n''<sub>1</sub>]<sub>''q''</sub>[''n''<sub>2</sub>]<sub>''r''</sub>), the number of vertices is ''g''/''g''<sub>2</sub>, and the number of faces is ''g''/''g''<sub>1</sub>. The number of edges is ''g''/''pr''.

=== Enumeration of regular complex 4-polytopes ===

==== Visualizations of regular complex 4-polytopes ====
<gallery>
4-simplex t0.svg|Real [[5-cell|{3,3,3}]], {{CDD|node_1|3|node|3|node|3|node}}, had 5 vertices, 10 edges, 10 {3} faces, and 5 {3,3} cells
24-cell t0 F4.svg|Real [[24-cell|{3,4,3}]], {{CDD|node_1|3|node|4|node|3|node}}, had 24 vertices, 96 edges, 96 {3} faces, and 24 {3,4} cells

600-cell graph H4.svg|Real [[600-cell|{3,3,5}]], {{CDD|node_1|3|node|3|node|5|node}}, had 120 vertices, 720 edges, 1200 {3} faces, and 600 {3,3} cells
Witting_polytope.png|[[Witting polytope]], {{CDD|3node_1|3|3node|3|3node|3|3node}}, has 240 vertices, 2160 3-edges, 2160 3{3}3 faces, and 240 3{3}3{3}3 cells
</gallery>

;Generalized 4-orthoplexes
Generalized 4-orthoplexes have a regular construction as {{CDD|node_1|3|node|3|node|4|pnode}} and quasiregular form as {{CDD|node_1|3|node|3split1|branch|labelp}}. All elements are [[simplex]]es.
<gallery>
Complex multipartite graph 16-cell.svg|Real [[16-cell|{3,3,4}]], {{CDD|node_1|3|node|3|node|4|node}} or {{CDD|node_1|3|node|split1|nodes}}, with 8 vertices, 24 edges, 32 faces, and 16 cells

;Generalized 4-cubes

Generalized tesseracts have a regular construction as {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|3|node|3|node}} and prismatic construction as {{CDD|pnode_1|2c|pnode_1|2c|pnode_1|2c|pnode_1}}, a product of four ''p''-gonal 1-polytopes. Elements are lower dimensional generalized cubes.

=== Enumeration of regular complex 5-polytopes ===

=== Enumeration of regular complex apeirotopes ===
Coxeter enumerated this list of nonstarry regular complex apeirotopes or honeycombs.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=180|at=Table VI. The regular honeycombs}}

For each dimension there are 12 apeirotopes symbolized as &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|n+1}} exists in any dimensions <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math>, or <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> if ''p''=''q''=2. Coxeter calls these generalized cubic honeycombs for ''n''>2.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=174}}

Each has proportional element counts given as:
:k-faces = <math> {n \choose k}p^{n-k}r^k </math>, where <math>{n \choose m}=\frac{n!}{m!\,(n-m)!}</math> and ''n''! denotes the [[factorial]] of ''n''.

==== Regular complex 1-polytopes ====
The only regular complex 1-polytope is <sub>&infin;</sub>{}, or {{CDD|infinnode_1}}. Its real representation is an [[apeirogon]], {&infin;}, or {{CDD|node_1|infin|node}}.

==== Regular complex apeirogons ====
[[File:Rank2 infinite shephard subgroups.png|thumb|Some subgroups of the apeirogonal Shephard groups]]
[[File:Complex_apeirogon_chart2.png|thumb|11 complex apeirogons <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub>  with edge interiors colored in light blue, and edges around one vertex are colored individually. Vertices are shown as small black squares. Edges are seen as ''p''-sided regular polygons and vertex figures are ''r''-gonal.]]
[[File:7_quasiregular_complex_apeirogons.png|thumb|A quasiregular apeirogon {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode_1}} is a mixture of two regular apeirogons {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode}} and {{CDD|pnode|q|rnode_1}}, seen here with blue and pink edges. {{CDD|6node_1|3|6node_1}} has only one color of edges because ''q'' is odd, making it a double covering.]]
Rank 2 complex apeirogons have symmetry <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''r''</sub>, where 1/''p'' + 2/''q'' + 1/''r'' = 1. Coxeter expresses them as &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|2}} where ''q'' is constrained to satisfy {{math|''q'' {{=}} 2/(1 – (''p'' + ''r'')/''pr'')}}.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=111,136|at=and Table VI. The regular honeycombs}}

There are 8 solutions: 
{| class=wikitable
|<sub>2</sub>[&infin;]<sub>2</sub>||<sub>3</sub>[12]<sub>2</sub>||<sub>4</sub>[8]<sub>2</sub>||<sub>6</sub>[6]<sub>2</sub>||<sub>3</sub>[6]<sub>3</sub>||<sub>6</sub>[4]<sub>3</sub>||<sub>4</sub>[4]<sub>4</sub>||<sub>6</sub>[3]<sub>6</sub> 
|- align=center
|{{CDD|node|infin|node}}||{{CDD|3node|12|node}}||{{CDD|4node|8|node}}||{{CDD|6node|6|node}}||{{CDD|3node|6|3node}}||{{CDD|6node|4|3node}}||{{CDD|4node|4|4node}}||{{CDD|6node|3|6node}}
|}

There are two excluded solutions odd ''q'' and unequal ''p'' and ''r'': <sub>10</sub>[5]<sub>2</sub> and <sub>12</sub>[3]<sub>4</sub>, or  {{CDD|10node|5|node}} and  {{CDD|12node|3|4node}}.

A regular complex apeirogon <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> has ''p''-edges and ''r''-gonal vertex figures. The dual apeirogon of <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> is <sub>''r''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''</sub>. An apeirogon of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''p''</sub> is self-dual. Groups of the form <sub>''p''</sub>[2''q'']<sub>2</sub> have a half symmetry <sub>''p''</sub>[''q'']<sub>''p''</sub>, so a regular apeirogon {{CDD|pnode_1|2x|q|node}} is the same as quasiregular {{CDD|pnode_1|q|pnode_1}}.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=178–179|at=Table IV. The regular polygons}}

Apeirogons can be represented on the [[Argand plane]] share four different vertex arrangements. Apeirogons of the form <sub>2</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> have a vertex arrangement as {''q''/2,''p''}. The form <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>2</sub> have vertex arrangement as r{''p'',''q''/2}. Apeirogons of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>''r''</sub> have vertex arrangements {''p'',''r''}.

Including affine nodes, and <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math>, there are 3 more infinite solutions: <sub>&infin;</sub>[2]<sub>&infin;</sub>, <sub>&infin;</sub>[4]<sub>2</sub>, <sub>&infin;</sub>[3]<sub>3</sub>, and {{CDD|infinnode_1|2|infinnode_1}}, {{CDD|infinnode_1|4|node}}, and {{CDD|infinnode_1|3|3node}}. The first is an index 2 subgroup of the second. The vertices of these apeirogons exist in <math>\mathbb{C}^1</math>.

==== Regular complex apeirohedra ====
There are 22 regular complex apeirohedra in <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math> of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{''a''}<sub>''q''</sub>{''b''}<sub>''r''</sub>. 8 are self-dual (''p''=''r'' and ''a''=''b''), while 14 exist as dual polytope pairs. Three are entirely real (''p''=''q''=''r''=2).

Coxeter symbolizes 12 of them as &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|3}} or <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub>{4}<sub>''r''</sub> is the regular form of the product apeirotope &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|2}} × &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|2}} or <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub> × <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub>, where ''q'' is determined from ''p'' and ''r''.

{{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|4|qnode}} is the same as {{CDD|pnode_1|3split1-44|branch|labelq}}, as well as {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode}}, for ''p'',''r''=2,3,4,6. Also {{CDD|pnode_1|4|pnode|4|node}} = {{CDD|pnode|4|node_1|4|pnode}}.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=140}}

==== Regular complex 3-apeirotopes ====
There are 16 regular complex apeirotopes in <math>\mathbb{C}^3</math>. Coxeter expresses 12 of them by &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|3}} where ''q'' is constrained to satisfy {{math|''q'' {{=}} 2/(1 – (''p'' + ''r'')/''pr'')}}. These can also be decomposed as product apeirotopes: {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|3|node|4|rnode}} = {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode}}. The first case is the <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> [[cubic honeycomb]].

==== Regular complex 4-apeirotopes ====
There are 15 regular complex apeirotopes in <math>\mathbb{C}^4</math>. Coxeter expresses 12 of them by &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|4}} where ''q'' is constrained to satisfy {{math|''q'' {{=}} 2/(1 – (''p'' + ''r'')/''pr'')}}. These can also be decomposed as product apeirotopes: {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|3|node|3|node|4|rnode}} = {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode}}. The first case is the <math>\mathbb{R}^4</math> [[tesseractic honeycomb]]. The [[16-cell honeycomb]] and [[24-cell honeycomb]] are real solutions. The last solution is generated has [[Witting polytope]] elements.

==== Regular complex 5-apeirotopes and higher ====
There are only 12 regular complex apeirotopes in <math>\mathbb{C}^5</math> or higher{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=146}} expressed &delta;{{supsub|''p'',''r''|n}} where ''q'' is constrained to satisfy {{math|''q'' {{=}} 2/(1 – (''p'' + ''r'')/''pr'')}}. These can also be decomposed a product of ''n'' apeirogons: {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|3|node}} ... {{CDD|3|node|3|node|4|rnode}} = {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode}} ... {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode|2|pnode_1|q|rnode}}. The first case is the real <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> [[hypercube honeycomb]].

=== van Oss polygon ===
[[File:Van_Oss_square_hole_in_octahedron.png|left|175px|thumb|A red square ''van Oss polygon'' in the plane of an edge and center of a regular octahedron.]]

A '''van Oss polygon''' is a regular polygon in the plane (real plane <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>, or unitary plane <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math>) in which both an edge and the centroid of a regular polytope lie, and formed of elements of the polytope. Not all regular polytopes have Van Oss polygons.

For example, the van Oss polygons of a real [[octahedron]] are the three squares whose planes pass through its center. In contrast a [[cube]] does not have a van Oss polygon because the edge-to-center plane cuts diagonally across two square faces and the two edges of the cube which lie in the plane do not form a polygon.

Infinite honeycombs also have '''van Oss apeirogons'''. For example, the real [[square tiling]] and [[triangular tiling]] have [[apeirogon]]s {&infin;} van Oss apeirogons.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|p=141}}

If it exists, the ''van Oss polygon'' of regular complex polytope of the form <sub>''p''</sub>{''q''}<sub>''r''</sub>{''s''}<sub>''t''</sub>... has ''p''-edges.
{{clear}}

== Non-regular complex polytopes ==

=== Product complex polytopes ===
{| class=wikitable style="float:right; margin-left:10px; width:360px"
|+ Example of a product complex polytope
|- valign=top
|[[File:Complex_polygon_2x5_stereographic3.svg|180px]]<BR>Complex product polygon {{CDD|node_1|2|5node_1}} or {}×<sub>5</sub>{} has 10 vertices connected by 5 2-edges and 2 5-edges, with its real representation as a 3-dimensional [[pentagonal prism]].
|width=200|[[File:Dual complex polygon 2x5 perspective.png|120px|class=skin-invert]]<BR>The dual polygon,{}+<sub>5</sub>{} has 7 vertices centered on the edges of the original, connected by 10 edges. Its real representation is a [[pentagonal bipyramid]].
|}

Some complex polytopes can be represented as [[Cartesian product]]s. These product polytopes are not strictly regular since they'll have more than one facet type, but some can represent lower symmetry of regular forms if all the orthogonal polytopes are identical. For example, the product <sub>''p''</sub>{}×<sub>''p''</sub>{} or {{CDD|pnode_1|2|pnode_1}} of two 1-dimensional polytopes is the same as the regular <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub> or {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node}}. More general products, like <sub>''p''</sub>{}×<sub>''q''</sub>{} have real representations as the 4-dimensional ''p''-''q'' [[duoprism]]s. The dual of a product polytope can be written as a sum <sub>''p''</sub>{}+<sub>''q''</sub>{} and have real representations as the 4-dimensional ''p''-''q'' [[duopyramid]]. The <sub>''p''</sub>{}+<sub>''p''</sub>{} can have its symmetry doubled as a regular complex polytope <sub>2</sub>{4}<sub>''p''</sub> or {{CDD|node_1|4|pnode}}.

Similarly, a <math>\mathbb{C}^3</math> complex polyhedron can be constructed as a triple product: <sub>''p''</sub>{}×<sub>''p''</sub>{}×<sub>''p''</sub>{} or {{CDD|pnode_1|2c|pnode_1|2c|pnode_1}} is the same as the regular ''generalized cube'', <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub>{3}<sub>2</sub> or {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|3|node}}, as well as product <sub>''p''</sub>{4}<sub>2</sub>×<sub>''p''</sub>{} or {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|2|pnode_1}}.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=118–119,138}}

=== Quasiregular polygons ===
A [[quasiregular polyhedron|quasiregular]] polygon is a [[Truncation (geometry)|truncation]] of a regular polygon. A quasiregular polygon {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode_1}} contains alternate edges of the regular polygons {{CDD|pnode_1|q|rnode}} and {{CDD|pnode|q|rnode_1}}. The quasiregular polygon has ''p'' vertices on the p-edges of the regular form.

=== Quasiregular apeirogons ===
There are 7 quasiregular complex apeirogons which alternate edges of a [[#Regular_complex_1-polytopes|regular apeirogon]] and its regular dual. The [[vertex arrangement]]s of these apeirogon have real representations with the regular and uniform tilings of the [[Euclidean plane]]. The last column for the 6{3}6 apeirogon is not only self-dual, but the dual coincides with itself with overlapping hexagonal edges, thus their quasiregular form also has overlapping hexagonal edges, so it can't be drawn with two alternating colors like the others. The symmetry of the self-dual families can be doubled, so creating an identical geometry as the regular forms: {{CDD|pnode_1|q|pnode_1}} = {{CDD|pnode_1|2x|q|node}}

=== Quasiregular polyhedra ===
[[File:3-generalized-octahedron_truncation_sequence.gif|thumb|Example truncation of 3-generalized octahedron, <sub>2</sub>{3}<sub>2</sub>{4}<sub>3</sub>, {{CDD|node_1|3|node|4|3node}}, to its rectified limit, showing outlined-green triangles faces at the start, and blue <sub>2</sub>{4}<sub>3</sub>, {{CDD|node_1|4|3node}}, vertex figures expanding as new faces.]]
Like real polytopes, a complex quasiregular polyhedron can be constructed as a [[rectification (geometry)|rectification]] (a complete [[truncation (geometry)|truncation]]) of a [[regular polyhedron]]. Vertices are created mid-edge of the regular polyhedron and faces of the regular polyhedron and its dual are positioned alternating across common edges.

For example, a p-generalized cube, {{CDD|pnode_1|4|node|3|node}}, has ''p''<sup>3</sup> vertices, 3''p''<sup>2</sup> edges, and 3''p'' ''p''-generalized square faces, while the ''p''-generalized octahedron, {{CDD|pnode|4|node|3|node_1}}, has 3''p'' vertices, 3''p''<sup>2</sup> edges and ''p''<sup>3</sup> triangular faces. The middle quasiregular form ''p''-generalized cuboctahedron, {{CDD|pnode|4|node_1|3|node}}, has 3''p''<sup>2</sup> vertices, 3''p''<sup>3</sup> edges, and 3''p''+''p''<sup>3</sup> faces.

Also the [[rectification (geometry)|rectification]] of the [[Hessian polyhedron]] {{CDD|3node_1|3|3node|3|3node}}, is {{CDD|3node|3|3node_1|3|3node}}, a quasiregular form sharing the geometry of the regular complex polyhedron {{CDD|3node_1|3|3node|4|node}}.

=== Other complex polytopes with unitary reflections of period two ===
Other nonregular complex polytopes can be constructed within unitary reflection groups that don't make linear Coxeter graphs. In Coxeter diagrams with loops Coxeter marks a special period interior, like {{CDD|node_1|3split1|branch}} or symbol (1<sub>1</sub> 1 1)<sup>3</sup>, and group [1 1 1]<sup>3</sup>.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=156–174|at=Chapter 14, ''Almost regular polytopes''}}<ref name="Coxeter 1956">Coxeter (1956), ''Groups Generated by Unitary Reflections of Period Two'', Table III: Some Complex Polytopes, p. 413</ref> These complex polytopes have not been systematically explored beyond a few cases.

The group {{CDD|node|psplit1|branch}} is defined by 3 unitary reflections, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub>, all order 2: R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = R<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = R<sub>3</sub><sup>2</sup> = (R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>)<sup>3</sup> =  (R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>)<sup>3</sup> = (R<sub>3</sub>R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>3</sup> = (R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>R<sub>1</sub>)<sup>''p''</sup> = 1. The period ''p'' can be seen as a [[double rotation]] in real <math>\mathbb{R}^4</math>.

As with all [[Wythoff construction]]s, polytopes generated by reflections, the number of vertices of a single-ringed Coxeter diagram polytope is equal to the order of the group divided by the order of the subgroup where the ringed node is removed. For example, a real [[cube]] has Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_1|4|node|3|node}}, with [[octahedral symmetry]] {{CDD|node|4|node|3|node}} order 48, and subgroup dihedral symmetry {{CDD|node|3|node}} order 6, so the number of vertices of a cube is 48/6=8. Facets are constructed by removing one node furthest from the ringed node, for example {{CDD|node_1|4|node}} for the cube. [[Vertex figure]]s are generated by removing a ringed node and ringing one or more connected nodes, and {{CDD|node_1|3|node}} for the cube.

Coxeter represents these groups by the following symbols. Some groups have the same order, but a different structure, defining the same [[vertex arrangement]] in complex polytopes, but different edges and higher elements, like {{CDD|node|psplit1|branch}} and {{CDD|node|3split1|branch|labelp}} with ''p''≠3.<ref>[[Coxeter]] (1966), ''Finite Groups Generated by Unitary Reflections'', 4. ''The Graphical Notation'', Table of ''n''-dimensional groups generated by n Unitary Reflections. pp. 422–423</ref>

Coxeter calls some of these complex polyhedra ''almost regular'' because they have regular facets and vertex figures. The first is a lower symmetry form of the generalized cross-polytope in <math>\mathbb{C}^3</math>. The second is a fractional generalized cube, reducing ''p''-edges into single vertices leaving ordinary 2-edges. Three of them are related to the [[finite regular skew polyhedron]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^4</math>.

==== Visualizations ====
<gallery>
Complex_polyhedron_almost_regular_42_vertices.png|(1 1 1<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup>)<sup>4</sup>, {{CDD|node_1|4split1|branch|label4}} has 42 vertices, 168 edges and 112 triangular faces, seen in this 14-gonal projection.
Complex polyhedron almost regular 46 vertices.png|(1<sup>4</sup> 1<sup>4</sup> 1<sub>1</sub>)<sup>(3)</sup>, {{CDD|node_1|anti3split1-44|branch}} has 56 vertices, 168 edges and 84 square faces, seen in this 14-gonal projection.
Complex_4-polytope_almost_regular_80_vertices.png|(1 1 2<sub>2</sub>)<sup>4</sup>, {{CDD|node_1|3|node|4split1|branch}} has 80 vertices, 640 edges, 1280 triangular faces and 640 tetrahedral cells, seen in this 20-gonal projection.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1991|pp=172–173}}
</gallery>
